## What we asked

Thanos removed half of all life, chosen at random. As a plan for breaking a network, how
good was that? This week's tools — shortest paths, betweenness, null models — let us ask the
question properly: if you delete Marvel characters one at a time, which *order* fragments the
wiki-link universe fastest? Is any single character essential, in the sense that losing them
strands other characters? And is whatever we find a fact about Marvel, or just a fact about
any network with this degree sequence?

## Loading this week's release

No new dataset this week — the shared week-1 snapshot is reused as-is (303 characters, 1784
directed links, 17 isolates). Fragmentation is a question about who can still reach whom, so we
drop direction and work on the undirected giant component.

```{python}
import random

import networkx as nx
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

%matplotlib inline

nodes = pd.read_csv("data/week3_nodes.tsv", sep="\t", comment="#", quoting=3)
edges = pd.read_csv("data/week3_edges.tsv", sep="\t", comment="#", names=["source", "target"])

graph = nx.DiGraph()
graph.add_nodes_from(nodes.node_id)
graph.add_edges_from(edges.itertuples(index=False))
name_lookup = dict(zip(nodes.node_id, nodes.name))

g = graph.to_undirected()
g.remove_edges_from(nx.selfloop_edges(g))
giant = g.subgraph(max(nx.connected_components(g), key=len)).copy()
N = giant.number_of_nodes()


def gc_size(h):
    return max((len(c) for c in nx.connected_components(h)), default=0)


print(f"Giant component: {N} characters, {giant.number_of_edges()} links")
```

## The snap, versus a strategy

One function, five removal orders. "Static" orders rank everyone once on the intact network
and work down the list; "adaptive" orders re-rank after every removal, which is what an
attacker who can see the damage they've done would actually do.

```{python}
def attack(h, strategy, stop_frac=0.55, seed=0):
    """Remove nodes one at a time. Returns giant-component sizes (index 0 = intact) and a log of (node, degree at removal)."""
    h = h.copy()
    n0 = h.number_of_nodes()
    sizes, log = [gc_size(h)], []
    if strategy == "random":
        order = list(h.nodes())
        random.Random(seed).shuffle(order)
    elif strategy == "degree":
        order = sorted(h.nodes(), key=lambda n: -h.degree(n))
    elif strategy == "betweenness":
        b = nx.betweenness_centrality(h)
        order = sorted(h.nodes(), key=lambda n: -b[n])
    for step in range(int(stop_frac * n0)):
        if strategy == "adaptive degree":
            v = max(h.degree(), key=lambda kv: kv[1])[0]
        elif strategy == "adaptive betweenness":
            b = nx.betweenness_centrality(h)
            v = max(b, key=b.get)
        else:
            v = order[step]
        log.append((v, h.degree(v)))
        h.remove_node(v)
        sizes.append(gc_size(h))
    return np.array(sizes), log


def halving_point(sizes):
    """Number of removals until the giant component is at most half its starting size."""
    return int(np.argmax(sizes <= sizes[0] / 2))


strategies = ["degree", "betweenness", "adaptive degree", "adaptive betweenness"]
curves = {s: attack(giant, s) for s in strategies}
random_runs = [attack(giant, "random", seed=s)[0] for s in range(20)]
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-collapse
#| fig-cap: "Giant-component size as characters are removed, by removal order. The dashed line is what you'd see if the network never fragmented at all — the giant component shrinking only because people are gone. The random snap sits on it."

x = np.arange(len(random_runs[0])) / N
rand = np.array(random_runs) / N

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 5))
ax.plot(x, 1 - x, "--", color="gray", linewidth=1, label="no fragmentation (1 − removed)")
ax.fill_between(x, rand.min(axis=0), rand.max(axis=0), color="#999999", alpha=0.3)
ax.plot(x, rand.mean(axis=0), color="#555555", linewidth=2, label="random snap (20 runs)")
colors = {"degree": "#4c72b0", "betweenness": "#55a868", "adaptive degree": "#8172b2", "adaptive betweenness": "#c8102e"}
for s in strategies:
    ax.plot(x, curves[s][0] / N, color=colors[s], linewidth=2, label=s)
ax.set_xlabel("fraction of characters removed")
ax.set_ylabel("giant component (fraction of original)")
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.02)
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
rows = [("random snap (mean of 20)", np.mean([halving_point(r) for r in random_runs]))]
rows += [(s, halving_point(curves[s][0])) for s in strategies]
halving = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["removal order", "removals to halve the giant component"])
halving["share of characters"] = (halving.iloc[:, 1] / N).map("{:.0%}".format)
halving
```

```{python}
half = int(np.ceil(N / 2))
snap_gc = np.mean([r[half] for r in random_runs])
print(f"Snap {half} of {N} at random: {N - half} survivors, {snap_gc:.0f} of them still in one connected piece")
k = halving_point(curves["adaptive betweenness"][0])
print(f"Remove {k} by adaptive betweenness: {N - k} survivors, {curves['adaptive betweenness'][0][k]} of them still in one connected piece")
```

The snap curve is the dashed diagonal, give or take a few characters. Snap exactly half the
cast — 139 of 277, at random — and 125 of the 138 survivors are still in one connected piece;
thirteen people get stranded. Thanos halved the population and fragmented almost nothing.
Ranking by degree or betweenness once and working down the list gets the giant component to
half its size with 81 removals; re-ranking after every removal gets it there with 63, or 23% of
the cast — and this time 76 of the 214 survivors are cut off from the main body, in 41
separate pieces. Same giant component, a very different universe.

Sixty-three is the honest headline number, and it's not a small one. The textbook picture of a
scale-free network is one that shatters when you pull a handful of hubs. This one doesn't:
there are enough links among the non-hubs that you have to delete a quarter of the universe,
chosen as cleverly as we know how, to break it in half.

Or run the snap yourself — the slider replays every removal order from the figure above:

## The hit list

Who does the adaptive attacker actually remove, and how far does that list drift from the
fame ranking?

```{python}
degree = dict(giant.degree())
static_bet = nx.betweenness_centrality(giant)
degree_rank = {n: r + 1 for r, n in enumerate(sorted(giant.nodes(), key=lambda n: -degree[n]))}
bet_rank = {n: r + 1 for r, n in enumerate(sorted(giant.nodes(), key=lambda n: -static_bet[n]))}

hit_list = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        (i + 1, name_lookup[v], d, degree[v], degree_rank[v], bet_rank[v])
        for i, (v, d) in enumerate(curves["adaptive betweenness"][1][:12])
    ],
    columns=["step", "character", "degree when removed", "original degree", "degree rank", "betweenness rank"],
)
hit_list
```

For six steps the attacker and the fame ranking agree exactly: Spider-Man, Hulk, Wolverine,
Doctor Strange, Deadpool, She-Hulk — degree ranks 1 through 6, in order. Step 7 is where they
part. Hercules, degree rank 20, gets pulled forward thirteen places: with the hubs gone, his
bridge to the mythology characters is one of the few routes left between that corner and the
rest. From there the list stops looking like a popularity contest — Cloak and Dagger (degree
rank 13), Quasar (26), Hank Pym (16) — while Scarlet Witch, 32 links and degree rank 8, isn't
touched in the first twelve. The "degree when removed" column is the tell: by step 11 the
attacker is deleting characters with 24 links, because they carry more of the *remaining*
shortest paths than Scarlet Witch's 32 do.

## Nobody is essential

The attack curves say the network is hard to break by attrition. Single removals are the
sharper version of the question: is there any one character whose deletion cuts other
characters off entirely?

```{python}
articulation = set(nx.articulation_points(giant))
stranded = []
for v in articulation:
    h = giant.copy()
    h.remove_node(v)
    stranded.append((name_lookup[v], degree[v], bet_rank[v], N - 1 - gc_size(h)))

stranded = pd.DataFrame(stranded, columns=["character", "degree", "betweenness rank", "characters stranded"])
stranded = stranded.sort_values("characters stranded", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
print(f"{len(articulation)} of {N} characters strand anyone at all when removed")
stranded
```

Thirteen. The other 264 can vanish one at a time and every remaining character still reaches
every other. Spider-Man — degree 106, betweenness rank 1 — is the most damaging single
removal, and he strands *five people*. Black Widow, degree 25, strands three, which is the
number that made us look twice: more than Doctor Strange (degree 57, two), and more than Hulk
or Wolverine, who have 65 and 63 links and strand one at most.

That's the same Black Widow who showed up last time we compared betweenness to a null model.
Betweenness rewards having lots of links as much as it rewards sitting between things, so we
scored every character against 200 shuffled copies of the network that keep everyone's exact
degree and rewire the rest:

```{python}
#| label: fig-zscore
#| fig-cap: "Betweenness z-score (real vs. 200 degree-preserving shuffles) against degree. Points far above zero broker more than their degree alone predicts."

random.seed(42)
m = giant.number_of_edges()
samples = {n: [] for n in giant.nodes()}
for _ in range(200):
    gs = giant.copy()
    try:
        nx.double_edge_swap(gs, nswap=m, max_tries=m * 10, seed=random.randint(0, 10**9))
    except nx.NetworkXAlgorithmError:
        pass
    bs = nx.betweenness_centrality(gs)
    for n in giant.nodes():
        samples[n].append(bs[n])


def zscore(real, s):
    arr = np.array(s)
    return (real - arr.mean()) / arr.std() if arr.std() > 0 else np.nan


z = {n: zscore(static_bet[n], samples[n]) for n in giant.nodes()}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
ok = [n for n in giant.nodes() if not np.isnan(z[n])]
ax.scatter([degree[n] for n in ok], [z[n] for n in ok], alpha=0.5, s=18, color="#4c72b0")
ax.axhline(0, color="gray", linewidth=0.8)
for query in ["Hercules", "Black Widow"]:
    node_id = nodes[nodes["name"].str.contains(query, case=False, na=False)].iloc[0]["node_id"]
    ax.scatter([degree[node_id]], [z[node_id]], color="#c8102e", s=40, zorder=5)
    ax.annotate(query, (degree[node_id], z[node_id]), fontsize=9, fontweight="bold",
                xytext=(6, 4), textcoords="offset points")
ax.set_xlabel("degree")
ax.set_ylabel("betweenness z-score vs. degree-preserving null")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
stranded_by = dict(zip(stranded["character"], stranded["characters stranded"]))
brokers = sorted(ok, key=lambda n: -z[n])[:6]
pd.DataFrame(
    [(name_lookup[n], degree[n], round(z[n], 2), bet_rank[n], stranded_by.get(name_lookup[n], 0)) for n in brokers],
    columns=["character", "degree", "betweenness z-score", "betweenness rank", "characters stranded"],
)
```

Black Widow and Hercules are the two characters whose betweenness is furthest above what their
degree predicts — 3.9 and 3.8 standard deviations above the shuffles, with degrees of 25 and
26 that don't crack the top ten by any "how connected are you" measure. (Further down the
list, Ikaris and Nightmask manage a z-score above 3 with *five* links each. Being a
statistically unusual broker is cheap.) They're genuine
brokers: their links sit on routes between clusters (Avengers-core and the espionage crowd for
Black Widow; Avengers-core and the classical-mythology characters for Hercules) that would
otherwise take the long way round. But brokerage and essentiality turn out to be different
things. Black Widow's bridge is a real one — cut it and three characters fall off. Hercules's
isn't: remove him and everyone he "bridges" still reaches everyone else, just one hop later.
High betweenness tells you a lot of shortest paths *currently* go through someone. It doesn't
tell you there's no second-shortest path.

## Compared to what

Twenty-three percent is a robust network, but robust compared to what? Two nulls, attacked the
same way: degree-preserving shuffles of Marvel (same characters, same degrees, links rewired at
random) and `G(n, m)` random graphs with the same number of nodes and links but no hubs at all.

```{python}
def null_attack(h, label):
    giant_h = h.subgraph(max(nx.connected_components(h), key=len)).copy()
    adaptive, _ = attack(giant_h, "adaptive betweenness", stop_frac=0.5)
    rand = attack(giant_h, "random", stop_frac=0.55)[0]
    n_h = giant_h.number_of_nodes()
    return {"null": label, "nodes": n_h, "adaptive": adaptive, "random": rand,
            "adaptive %": halving_point(adaptive) / n_h, "random %": halving_point(rand) / n_h}


null_runs = []
for s in range(5):
    shuffled = giant.copy()
    nx.double_edge_swap(shuffled, nswap=m, max_tries=m * 10, seed=s)
    null_runs.append(null_attack(shuffled, "degree-preserving shuffle"))
    null_runs.append(null_attack(nx.gnm_random_graph(N, m, seed=s), "G(n, m) random graph"))

def spread(runs, key):
    vals = [r[key] for r in runs]
    return f"{np.mean(vals):.1%}  ({min(vals):.1%} – {max(vals):.1%})"


rows = [("Marvel", f"{halving_point(curves['adaptive betweenness'][0]) / N:.1%}",
         f"{np.mean([halving_point(r) for r in random_runs]) / N:.1%}  (mean of 20)")]
for label in ["degree-preserving shuffle", "G(n, m) random graph"]:
    runs = [r for r in null_runs if r["null"] == label]
    rows.append((f"{label} (5 runs)", spread(runs, "adaptive %"), spread(runs, "random %")))
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["network", "adaptive betweenness attack: share removed to halve", "random snap: share removed to halve"])
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-null-collapse
#| fig-cap: "The adaptive-betweenness attack on Marvel (red) against the same attack on five degree-preserving shuffles (blue) and five G(n, m) random graphs (green)."

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 5))
for run in null_runs:
    xs = np.arange(len(run["adaptive"])) / run["nodes"]
    color = "#4c72b0" if run["null"].startswith("degree") else "#55a868"
    ax.plot(xs, run["adaptive"] / run["nodes"], color=color, alpha=0.6, linewidth=1.2)
ax.plot([], [], color="#4c72b0", label="degree-preserving shuffles")
ax.plot([], [], color="#55a868", label="G(n, m) random graphs")
marvel = curves["adaptive betweenness"][0]
ax.plot(np.arange(len(marvel)) / N, marvel / N, color="#c8102e", linewidth=2.5, label="Marvel")
ax.axhline(0.5, color="gray", linewidth=0.8, linestyle=":")
ax.set_xlabel("fraction of characters removed (adaptive betweenness order)")
ax.set_ylabel("giant component (fraction of original)")
ax.set_xlim(0, 0.5)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.02)
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Marvel breaks *sooner* than its own shuffles: 22.7% of the cast, against 27.3% (25.6–28.2%
across five rewirings) for networks with exactly the same characters and exactly the same
degrees — about thirteen fewer removals. So the robustness we found above is actually the
degree sequence being *generous*; Marvel's real wiring gives some of it back. The random snap
doesn't care about any of this: 46% for Marvel, 47% for the shuffles, 50% for `G(n, m)`.
Attrition is a degree-sequence property and nothing else.

The hub-free random graphs are the other half of the answer. There, the adaptive attack needs
46% — barely better than snapping at random, because with every character at roughly the same
degree there is nothing worth targeting. Hubs are what make a targeted attack work at all. And
the specific way Marvel's links are arranged — teams, families, and the brokers who connect
them — is what makes it work five points better than the degrees alone predict. Rewire those
same links at random and the seams the attacker was cutting along stop existing.

## What surprised us

Not that a targeted attack beats a random one — that's the whole point of centrality. What
surprised us is the scale on both ends. Thanos's snap, at exactly half the cast, strands
thirteen people; the other 125 survivors are as connected as they ever were. And the best
attack we could build still needs 63 deletions, nearly a quarter of the universe, to halve the
giant component — no single one of them strands more than five, and the network's second most
statistically unusual broker, Hercules, strands none. Black Widow is the odd one out: a broker
by the null model *and* the second most damaging single removal in the network, at degree 25.
The part we didn't expect at all is the null: a random rewiring of Marvel with the same degrees
is *harder* to break than Marvel. Whatever structure the wiki-link universe has beyond its
degree sequence, it isn't there to protect it.
